# High-Level Language Idioms in Assembly Language {#appendix-e-c-idioms-in-assembly-language}

This appendix is for programmers of high-level languages learning
assembly language. It is meant to give a general idea about how the
constructs of those languages can be implemented in assembly language.
The examples are in Rust, but C, Go, Java and most other languages have
the same constructs, and their compilers translate them in the same
way.

If Statement {#if-statement}
------------

An if statement consists of three parts - the condition, the true
branch, and the false branch. However, since assembly language is not a
block structured language, you have to work a little to implement the
block-like nature of an if. For example, look at the following Rust
code:

```{.rust}
if a == b {
    // True branch code here.
} else {
    // False branch code here.
}

// At this point, reconverge.
```

In assembly language, this can be rendered as:

```{.gnuassembler}
    movq  a(%rip), %rax     # Move a and b into registers
    movq  b(%rip), %rbx     # for comparison.

    cmpq  %rax, %rbx        # Compare.

    je    true_branch       # If true, go to true branch.

false_branch:               # This label is unnecessary,
                            # only here for documentation.
                            # False branch code here.

    jmp   reconverge        # Jump to reconvergence point.

true_branch:                # True branch code here.

reconverge:                 # Both branches reconverge to
                            # this point.
```

As you can see, since assembly language is linear, the blocks have to
jump around each other. Reconvergence is handled by the programmer, not
the system.

A `match` (or a `switch` in C) is written just like a sequence of if
statements. When the cases are consecutive numbers, compilers often
build a *jump table* instead: a list of addresses, one per case, and an
indirect jump, `jmp *(%rbx,%rax,8)`, to the one for the value in _%rax_.

An if that only chooses a value, such as
`let largest = if item > largest { item } else { largest };`, can be
written without any jump, with a conditional move, as `rustc` did in
[Chapter 11](11-high-level-languages.qmd#what-the-compiler-generates):

```{.gnuassembler}
    cmpq  %rax, %rcx        # item (%rcx) > largest (%rax)?
    cmovgq %rcx, %rax       # Then largest = item.
```

Function Call {#function-call}
-------------

A function call in assembly language simply requires putting the
arguments to the function in the registers of the calling convention,
in order - _%rdi_, _%rsi_, _%rdx_, _%rcx_, _%r8_ and _%r9_ (the rest go
on the stack) - and issuing a `call` instruction, with _%rsp_ aligned to
16. The result comes back in _%rax_. For example, consider the Rust
code:

```{.rust}
let total = add(88, 12);
```

In assembly language, this would be rendered as:

```{.gnuassembler}
    movq  $88, %rdi         # First argument.
    movq  $12, %rsi         # Second argument.
    call  add
    movq  %rax, %rbx        # The result. %rbx is
                            # callee-saved, so it survives
                            # the next calls.
```

A call to a function with a variable number of arguments, such as the C
library\'s `printf`, also needs the number of vector registers used in
_%al_:

```{.gnuassembler}
.section .data
    text_string:
        .ascii "The number is %ld\n\0"

.section .text
    leaq  text_string(%rip), %rdi
    movq  $88, %rsi
    movq  $0, %rax          # No floating-point arguments.
    call  printf@PLT
```

Variables and Assignment {#variables-and-assignment}
------------------------

Global and static variables are declared using `.data` or `.bss` entries.
Local variables are declared by reserving space on the stack at the
beginning of the function. This space is given back at the end of the
function.

Interestingly, global variables are accessed differently than local
variables in assembly language. Global variables are accessed relative
to _%rip_, while local variables are accessed using base pointer
addressing mode. For example, consider the following Rust code:

```{.rust}
static mut MY_GLOBAL_VAR: i64 = 0;

fn foo() -> i64 {
    let my_local_var: i64;

    my_local_var = 1;
    unsafe { MY_GLOBAL_VAR = 2; }

    0
}
```

This would be rendered in assembly language as:

```{.gnuassembler}
    .section .bss
        .lcomm my_global_var, 8

    .section .text
    .type  foo,  @function
foo:
    pushq %rbp              # Save old base pointer.
    movq  %rsp, %rbp        # Make stack pointer base
                            # pointer.
    subq  $16, %rsp         # Make room for my_local_var
                            # (16 bytes, to keep %rsp
                            # aligned).
    .equ my_local_var, -8   # Can now use my_local_var
                            # to find the local
                            # variable.

    movq  $1, my_local_var(%rbp)
    movq  $2, my_global_var(%rip)

    movq  $0, %rax          # The result.

    movq  %rbp, %rsp        # Clean up function and
    popq  %rbp              # return.
    ret
```

Rust makes you write `unsafe` to change a `static mut`, because two
threads could change it at the same time; the assembly language version
has the same problem, but nobody warns you.

Also note that in compiled languages, after the compiler loads a value
into a register, that value will likely stay in that register until
that register is needed for something else. It may also move registers.
For example, if you have a variable `foo`, it may start on the stack,
but the compiler will eventually move it into registers for processing.
If there aren\'t many variables in use, the value may simply stay in the
register until it is needed again, and with optimizations, most local
variables never get a place on the stack at all. Otherwise, when that
register is needed for something else, the value, if it\'s changed, is
copied back to its corresponding memory location. If another thread or
some hardware may change a memory location while your function is
running, the compiler must be told, so that it reads the memory every
time: in Rust with atomic types (`AtomicI64`) or `read_volatile`, and in
C with the keyword `volatile`.

Loops {#loops}
-----

Loops work a lot like if statements in assembly language - the
blocks are formed by jumping around. A while loop consists of a loop
body, and a test to determine whether or not it is time to exit the
loop. A for loop over a range is exactly the same, with an
initialization and a counter-increment. These can simply be moved around
to make a while loop.

In Rust, a while loop looks like this:

```{.rust}
while a < b {
    // Do stuff here.
}

// Finished looping.
```

This can be rendered in assembly language like this:

```{.gnuassembler}
loop_begin:
    movq  a(%rip), %rax
    movq  b(%rip), %rbx
    cmpq  %rbx, %rax        # a < b?
    jge   loop_end          # If not, we are done.

loop_body:                  # Do stuff here.

    jmp   loop_begin

loop_end:                   # Finished looping.
```

The x86-64 assembly language has some direct support for looping as
well. The _%rcx_ register can be used as a counter that *ends* with
zero. The `loop` instruction will decrement _%rcx_ and jump to a
specified address unless _%rcx_ is zero. For example, if you wanted to
execute a statement 100 times, you would do this in Rust:

```{.rust}
for i in 0..100 {
    // Do process here.
}
```

In assembly language it could be written like this:

```{.gnuassembler}
loop_initialize:
    movq  $100, %rcx

loop_begin:                 # Do process here.
    loop  loop_begin        # Decrement %rcx and loop
                            # if not zero.

rest_of_program:            # Continues on to here.
```

One thing to notice is that the `loop` instruction *requires you to be
counting backwards to zero*. If you need to count forwards or use
another ending number, you should use the loop form which does not
include the `loop` instruction. In practice, compilers never use `loop`:
on current processors, `decq %rcx` followed by `jnz loop_begin` does the
same and is faster. And remember that a `syscall` overwrites _%rcx_.

For really tight loops of character string operations, there is also the
`rep` prefix (for example `rep movsb`, which copies _%rcx_ bytes from
the address in _%rsi_ to the address in _%rdi_), but we will leave
learning about that as an exercise to the reader.

Structs {#structs}
-------

Structs are simply descriptions of memory blocks. For example, in Rust
you can say:

```{.rust}
#[repr(C)]
struct Person {
    firstname: [u8; 40],
    lastname: [u8; 40],
    age: i64,
}
```

This doesn\'t do anything by itself, except give you ways of
intelligently using 88 bytes of data. `#[repr(C)]` asks Rust to keep the
fields in this order, with the layout of the calling convention, so the
offsets are the ones you would compute by hand (without it, Rust may
reorder the fields to waste less space). You can do basically the same
thing using `.equ` directives in assembly language, as Chapter 6 did
for its records. Like this:

```{.gnuassembler}
.equ PERSON_FIRSTNAME_OFFSET,  0
.equ PERSON_LASTNAME_OFFSET,   40
.equ PERSON_AGE_OFFSET,        80
.equ PERSON_SIZE,              88
```

When you declare a variable of this type, all you are doing is reserving
88 bytes of space. So, if you have this in Rust:

```{.rust}
fn foo() {
    let mut p: Person;

    // Do stuff here.
}
```

In assembly language you would have:

```{.gnuassembler}
foo:                        # Standard header beginning.
    pushq %rbp
    movq  %rsp, %rbp

    subq  $96, %rsp         # Reserve our local variable
                            # (88 bytes, rounded up to a
                            # multiple of 16).
    .equ P_VAR, -96         # This is the variable's
                            # offset from %rbp.

                            # Do stuff here.

    movq  %rbp, %rsp        # Standard function ending.
    popq  %rbp
    ret
```

To access structure members, you just have to use base pointer addressing
mode with the offsets defined above. For example, in Rust you could set
the person\'s age like this:

```{.rust}
p.age = 30;
```

In assembly language it would look like this:

```{.gnuassembler}
movq  $30, P_VAR + PERSON_AGE_OFFSET(%rbp)
```

Pointers {#pointers}
--------

Pointers are very easy. Remember, pointers are simply the address that a
value resides at. In Rust, the safe kind of pointer is called a
*reference*. Let\'s start by taking a look at global variables. For
example:

```{.rust}
static GLOBAL_DATA: i64 = 30;
```

In assembly language, this would be (in `.rodata`, because a `static`
without `mut` can\'t change):

```{.gnuassembler}
.section .rodata
    global_data:
        .quad 30
```

Taking the address of this data in Rust:

```{.rust}
let a = &GLOBAL_DATA;
```

Taking the address of this data in assembly language:

```{.gnuassembler}
leaq  global_data(%rip), %rax
```

You see, with assembly language, you are almost always accessing memory
through addresses. `movq global_data(%rip), %rax` reads the value, and
`leaq global_data(%rip), %rax` gives the address itself.

Local variables are a little more difficult, but not much. Here is how
you take the address of a local variable in Rust:

```{.rust}
fn foo() {
    let mut a: i64;
    let b: &mut i64;

    a = 30;

    b = &mut a;

    *b = 44;
}
```

The same code in assembly language:

```{.gnuassembler}
foo:
    pushq %rbp              # Standard opening.
    movq  %rsp, %rbp

    subq  $16, %rsp         # Reserve two quadwords of
    .equ A_VAR, -8          # memory.
    .equ B_VAR, -16

    movq  $30, A_VAR(%rbp)          # a = 30.

    movq  $A_VAR, B_VAR(%rbp)       # b = &a.
    addq  %rbp, B_VAR(%rbp)

    movq  B_VAR(%rbp), %rax         # *b = 44.
    movq  $44, (%rax)

    movq  %rbp, %rsp        # Standard closing.
    popq  %rbp
    ret
```

As you can see, to take the address of a local variable, the address has
to be computed the same way the computer computes the addresses in base
pointer addressing. There is an easier way - the processor provides the
instruction `leaq`, which stands for \"load effective address\". This
lets the computer compute the address, and then load it wherever you
want. So, we could just say:

```{.gnuassembler}
leaq  A_VAR(%rbp), %rax             # b = &a.
movq  %rax, B_VAR(%rbp)
```

It\'s the same number of lines, but a little cleaner. Then, to use this
value, you simply have to move it to a general-purpose register and use
indirect addressing mode, as shown in the example above.

What the Rust compiler adds is the checking: it doesn\'t let `b` live
longer than `a`, or let two `&mut` references to `a` exist at the same
time. In assembly language, nothing stops you from returning the address
of a local variable, whose memory is reused by the next function call.

Getting the Compiler to Help {#getting-the-compiler-to-help}
----------------------------

One of the nice things about compilers is their ability to spit out
assembly language code. As we saw in
[Chapter 11](11-high-level-languages.qmd#what-the-compiler-generates),
to convert a Rust file to assembly, you can simply do:

```{.bash}
rustc --edition 2024 --emit asm file.rs
```

The output will be in `file.s`. For a C file, `gcc -S file.c` does the
same. It\'s not the most readable output - most of the variable names
have been removed and replaced either with numeric stack locations or
references to automatically-generated labels. To start with, you
probably want to turn off optimizations with `-C opt-level=0` (`-O0`
for `gcc`) so that the assembly language output will follow your source
code better. [Compiler Explorer][AE-Godbolt] does all this in the web
browser, and colors each line of the source code and the instructions
that came from it.

Something else you might notice is that compilers often reserve more
stack space for local variables than we do, and some functions AND
_%rsp_ with a number like -16 or -32 (`andq $-32, %rsp`). This is to
align the stack for the variables that need it.[^AE-1]

Finally, at the end of functions, we usually do the following
instructions to clean up the stack before issuing a `ret`
instruction:

```{.gnuassembler}
movq  %rbp, %rsp
popq  %rbp
```

However, compiler output will usually just include the instruction
`leave`. This instruction is simply the combination of the above two
instructions. We do not use `leave` in this text because we want to be
clear about exactly what is happening at the processor level. And with
optimizations, as we saw, the compiler usually doesn\'t use _%rbp_ at
all (see
[The Frame Pointer](12-optimization.qmd#the-frame-pointer)).

I encourage you to take a program you have written and compile it to
assembly language and trace the logic. Then, add in optimizations and
try again. See how the compiler chose to rearrange your program to be
more optimized, and try to figure out why it chose the arrangement and
instructions it did.


[^AE-1]: Note that different compilers, and different versions of the
    same compiler, do this differently.

[AE-Godbolt]: https://godbolt.org/
